title: The rosary story
hook: tradition says Dominic received the rosary; historians say it grew over a long time, much loved by Dominicans

segments.voice: Yesterday, study as prayer: studium, zeal and devoted attention, offered for people. Your line was study is prayer. What did you give your full attention to? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

It's in paintings and stained glass and above side altars. A woman in blue, crowned, sits with a child on her lap. Kneeling below her is a friar in a white habit and a black cape. She leans down and hands him a string of beads. The friar is Dominic, the woman is Mary, and the beads are a rosary. It's a beautiful scene, and Dominicans have painted it lovingly. It also raises a question a curious person will eventually ask: did it happen like that? Today, the rosary story, and why the answer comes in two parts.
screen: `A WOMAN IN BLUE, A KNEELING FRIAR.` → `SHE HANDS HIM A STRING OF BEADS.` → `DID IT HAPPEN LIKE THAT?`

segments.voice: Part one is the tradition. Tradition says Mary gave the rosary to Dominic, as a help for his preaching in the south of France. Popes and preachers have retold it, and the picture hangs in Dominican churches. Part two is what historians see: a prayer that grew slowly, from many hands. Monks prayed the Psalms. People who couldn't read the Psalms prayed Our Fathers instead, counted on strings of beads or knots. Then came the Hail Mary, and its first lines are straight from Luke's Gospel, two greetings stitched together. The angel Gabriel's, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." And Elizabeth's, when Mary visits her: "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Over time people attached scenes to the beads, moments in the lives of Jesus and Mary to think about while the words went by. Those are the mysteries. And the Dominicans? Historians credit them with loving and spreading the rosary widely, preaching it and gathering people to pray it together; a later Dominican preacher also spread the story of Dominic receiving it. So Catholics hold this in different ways. Some take the story as history. Others read it as a picture of something true: the rosary found its home among Dominicans. Either way, the prayer itself is a story that grew, the way a family recipe grows, a pinch added by each generation, until nobody can say whose it was. It belongs to all of them.
screen: `TRADITION: MARY GIVES DOMINIC THE BEADS.` · `HISTORY: A PRAYER THAT GREW SLOWLY.` · `THE HAIL MARY BEGINS IN LUKE.` · `DOMINICANS LOVED IT AND SPREAD IT.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray one decade, or walk through its shape. If you have a rosary, hold it. If not, your fingers work. If you pray, begin with an Our Father, then a Hail Mary for each bead or finger, then a Glory Be, holding one scene in mind the whole time: Gabriel coming to Mary. If you don't pray, simply let each finger be one slow breath, and picture the scene: a young woman, a visitor, a word of greeting. Don't rush. Let the words, or the breaths, be the beads under the scene. The bell holds the time.
The rosary story. Tradition says Mary gave it to Dominic; historians see a prayer that grew slowly, loved and spread by Dominicans. Today's word.

Your line: a story that grew. Today, notice one thing in your own life that grew from many hands, a family saying, a song, a habit, and give thanks for the people who added to it. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary alone or together, often on beads, saying an Our Father, a decade of Hail Marys and a Glory Be while meditating on a mystery; Dominican friars and parishes lead it and preach about it.

fork.setup: you can't read, so you can't pray the Psalms the way the monks do. you still want a daily prayer with a steady rhythm. what do you do?
options: give up: prayer is for people who can read.
pray Our Fathers, counting them on a string of beads.

fork.reveal: historians see this as one of the roots of the rosary: simple prayers counted on beads or knots. the Hail Mary and the mysteries came later.

original.note: Latin: a rose garden. the prayer's name pictures a garland of prayers offered to Mary.

notes: The tradition that Mary gave the rosary to Dominic is widely linked to the preaching of Alan de la Roche (15th century); the voice says only 'a later Dominican preacher'. Confirm.
'Popes and preachers have retold it' (e.g., Leo XIII's rosary encyclicals) is stated without names; confirm.
The historical roots (Paternoster beads among those who could not read the Psalter; the Hail Mary; the mysteries attached later) are summarized without dates or counts. Confirm.
The practice avoids stating the number of Hail Marys in a decade under the claims rule; it says 'a Hail Mary for each bead or finger'. A Keeper may prefer 'ten'.
rosarium = rose garden (Lewis & Short); the garland image is traditional. Confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 1:28 and 1:42 to confirm.
